title: Function components

sources.locator: React Learn and Reference; React 19.2; provisions applicable to Function components
sources.claim: A function component receives props and returns renderable React nodes while remaining pure during render.

canonicalExplanation.summary: A **function component** is a JavaScript function, named with a Capital letter, that receives one object of **props** and **returns** what to show: JSX, a string, a number, null or a list of those. React may call it **many times**, once per render, and each call starts fresh: plain local variables don't survive between renders (that's what state is for). While rendering it must stay **pure**: same props give the same output, and it never changes props, globals or the DOM.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A course page repeats the same heading markup in five places, each slightly different. You want one reusable Greeting. A first attempt counts renders in a global variable and tweaks `props.name` to upper case, and the names start changing on other screens too. Greeting receives name and returns one heading without mutating props or external state. In this lesson you'll extract and test a cohesive component without hidden mutation.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Declarative UI and re-rendering**, **Text and page semantics** (headings and landmarks), and **Function declarations, expressions and arrows** (declarations, parameters and destructuring).

examples.title: A Greeting that only reads its props
examples.situation: Greeting receives name and returns one heading without mutating props or external state.
walkthrough: **Bug:** the old version did `props.name = props.name.toUpperCase()` and `renderCount++`, changing shared data.
**Pure version:** Greeting computes `display` from name and returns one heading; nothing outside is changed.
**Test:** rendering `<Greeting name="  " />` will show the heading "Welcome back, learner!" every time.
examples.result: Greeting shows the right heading everywhere it's used, and no other screen's names change.

examples.title: The list that doubled in StrictMode
examples.situation: A LessonList component does `allLessons.push(extraLesson)` on a module-level array before returning the list. In development the extra lesson appears twice.
walkthrough: StrictMode renders components twice in development to catch impure code.
Each render pushed into the shared array again.
Fix: build a new array during render: `const shown = [...allLessons, extraLesson]`.
examples.result: The list shows the extra lesson once, in development and production.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A component function runs once when mounted and retains its local variables forever.
misconceptions.correction: React calls a component function on every render. Local variables are created fresh each call, so anything that must persist between renders needs state or a ref.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why did the button keep showing 0?

analogy.example: A function component is like **a recipe card**: the same ingredients (props) always make the same dish (JSX). Cooking it again doesn't remember last time, and a good recipe never tells you to repaint the kitchen (change things outside).
limitations: Recipes are followed by people; React calls components whenever it needs.
State is the pantry that does remember between cooks.

steps.explanation: React calls Greeting with its props object.
Greeting receives name and computes a new value without mutating props.
It returns one heading and changes no external state.

trace.textAlternative:
One pure render of Greeting. Step 1, Call: props is { name: ' ' }; level is 2 (default). React calls Greeting with its props object. Step 2, Compute: display is 'learner'; props.name is unchanged. Greeting receives name and computes a new value without mutating props. Step 3, Return: output is

Welcome back, learner!

. It returns one heading and changes no external state.

remediation.explanation: Read your component and underline every line that **changes** something. Anything changing props, globals, the DOM or the network doesn't belong in the render body.

recap.summary: To extract and test a cohesive component without hidden mutation, write a capitalised function that receives props and returns JSX, compute new values instead of changing props or globals, remember React may call it many times, and test its rendered output.
